description: Write a regular expression and watch matches highlight live in your test text, with a full match list and capture-group breakdown. Supports all common flags and named groups, with built-in guards against runaway patterns.

faq.a: JavaScript's RegExp engine — the same one used in browsers and Node.js, including named capture groups.
To keep the page fast, output is capped at 200 matches. A warning appears if your pattern matched more.
No — everything runs locally in your browser. Nothing leaves your device.
faq.q: Is my pattern or text uploaded?

howTo: Type your regular expression in the pattern field.
Toggle flags like global (g), case-insensitive (i) or multiline (m).
Paste your test text and watch matches highlight instantly.
Expand the match list to inspect capture groups and named groups.
name: Regex Tester
tagline: Test patterns with live match highlighting

description: Paste any 5-field cron expression and get a plain-English explanation of when it runs, plus a per-field breakdown. Understands ranges, lists, steps, month/day names and @-shortcuts like @daily.

faq.a: Standard 5-field cron: minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week. Names like JAN or MON work, and so do @daily, @hourly and other shortcuts.
Every 15 units — in the minute field it means the job fires at :00, :15, :30 and :45.
Yes — both 0 and 7 are treated as Sunday, matching standard cron behaviour.
faq.q: Does it handle day 7 as Sunday?

howTo: Paste a 5-field cron expression (e.g. */15 9-17 * * 1-5).
Read the plain-English description at the top.
Check the per-field breakdown to see what each field means.
Try a preset button to explore common schedules.
name: Cron Describer

description: Convert Unix timestamps to UTC and local dates, or turn any date into its epoch value — in seconds or milliseconds. A one-click 'Use current time' button makes it effortless.

faq.a: 10-digit numbers are seconds, 13-digit are milliseconds. The tool shows both, so you can compare.
faq.q: Seconds or milliseconds — which do I have?

faq.a: Both: the UTC (ISO 8601) value and your browser's local time.
Yes — negative timestamps convert correctly to pre-1970 dates.

howTo: Choose the direction: timestamp to date, or date to timestamp.
Enter your value (or press 'Use current time').
Pick seconds or milliseconds for timestamp input.
Copy the ISO, UTC or epoch result you need.
name: Timestamp Converter

description: Generate MD5 hashes from any text or file with a pure JavaScript implementation — no uploads, no servers. Ideal for verifying file integrity and checksums.

faq.a: Never — the file is read and hashed entirely inside your browser.
No. MD5 is broken for password storage; use bcrypt or argon2. This tool is for checksums and integrity checks.
faq.q: Can I use MD5 for passwords?

faq.a: Yes — text is encoded as UTF-8 before hashing, so Urdu, emoji and all Unicode work.

howTo: Choose the Text or File tab.
Type your text or drop a file into the box.
The MD5 hash appears instantly.
Copy it, or toggle uppercase for comparison with other tools.
name: MD5 Hash Generator
tagline: MD5 checksums for text and files

description: Turn one-line SQL into clean, readable code: keywords are uppercased, major clauses start on new lines, and nested subqueries are indented. String literals are protected during formatting.

faq.a: No — it only adjusts whitespace and keyword case. Quoted strings and identifiers are left untouched.
faq.q: Will it change my query's meaning?

faq.a: It's dialect-agnostic and works with standard SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE plus common clauses and joins.
faq.q: Does it support all SQL dialects?

faq.a: No — formatting happens 100% in your browser.
faq.q: Is my query sent to a server?

howTo: Paste your SQL query into the input box.
Toggle 'Uppercase keywords' if you prefer lowercase.
The formatted query updates live.
Copy the result back into your editor or database client.
name: SQL Formatter

description: Minify CSS by stripping comments and collapsing whitespace, while carefully preserving strings and valid selector spacing. See before/after sizes and the percentage saved.

faq.a: The minifier is conservative: it never touches string contents or selector combinators, so valid input stays valid.
faq.q: Is the minified CSS guaranteed valid?

faq.a: Yes — spacing inside calc() and other functions is preserved.
Typically 15–30%, depending on how much whitespace and commenting your source had.
faq.q: How much smaller does CSS get?

howTo: Paste your CSS into the input box.
The minified output and size stats appear instantly.
Review the saved percentage.
Copy the minified CSS into your production stylesheet.
name: CSS Minifier

description: Paste tangled HTML and get it back neatly indented, with nested elements properly nested. Handles void elements, comments and self-closing tags, and warns about unclosed tags.

faq.a: No — it only adjusts indentation. Tags, attributes and text stay exactly as they were.
faq.q: Does it change my HTML structure?

faq.a: Yes — br, img, input, meta and other void elements never increase indentation.
It still indents what it can and warns you about tags that were never closed.
faq.q: What if my HTML is invalid?

howTo: Paste your HTML into the input box.
The indented version appears instantly.
Check for any unclosed-tag warnings.
Copy the clean markup.
name: HTML Indenter

description: Generate compact, URL-safe unique IDs using your browser's cryptographic random source. Choose the length and how many you need, then copy them one by one or all at once.

faq.a: A–Z, a–z, 0–9, hyphen and underscore — all safe in URLs and filenames.
Yes — they use crypto.getRandomValues, the browser's cryptographic random source.
With 21+ characters, collisions are practically impossible; each generation is independent.

howTo: Set the ID length with the slider (8–64 characters).
Choose how many IDs to generate (up to 50).
Click Generate.
Copy individual IDs or use 'Copy all'.
name: NanoID Generator

description: Check whether your text and background colours meet WCAG accessibility standards. Get the exact contrast ratio plus pass/fail badges for AA and AAA at normal and large text sizes.

faq.a: At least 4.5:1 for normal text (WCAG AA); 3:1 is the minimum for large text (18pt+ or 14pt bold).
faq.q: What ratio should I aim for?

faq.a: WCAG defines it as 18pt (24px) or 14pt (18.66px) bold and larger.
Using the WCAG relative-luminance formula — the same math auditors and browser dev tools use.

howTo: Pick a text color with the picker or type a HEX code.
Pick a background color the same way.
Preview your combination in the sample box.
Read the ratio and the AA/AAA badges.

name: Color Contrast Checker

description: Create placeholder PNG images at any size with your own background color, text color and label — rendered instantly on canvas. Preview and download the PNG for your mockups and wireframes.

faq.a: Anything from 1×1 up to 4096×4096 pixels.
PNG, generated directly from the canvas — crisp at any size.
No — it's drawn locally with the canvas API, so it works offline too.

howTo: Enter the width and height in pixels.
Pick background and text colors.
Type a custom label (or leave it to show the dimensions).
Download the generated PNG.
